title: I Mean…
subtitle: Four ways to explain yourself
review: Text by the author; notes and questions written by Claude: check them. No Burmese yet.
intro: A strange cake, a sweater that got smaller, a plant that is 'resting' and a couch with a spring sticking out: four short scenes between Emma and Lucas. Listen for the little phrases they use to correct themselves, explain again and buy time.

lines.text: So, what do you think of my cake?

lines.note: Different is a polite way to avoid saying 'bad'. I mean: he changes his word.
Or rather gives a more exact word.

lines.text: No, no, I do! Actually, what's in it?
lines.note: No, no, I do! = I do like it. Actually moves to the real question.
Zucchini is American English. British English: courgette.
Did the laundry: washed the clothes.

lines.text: Oh, that's sweet of you. Thanks.
lines.note: That's sweet of you = that's kind of you.

lines.text: Your blue sweater has… changed a little.

lines.note: What do you mean? asks him to explain.

lines.text: Well, it's a little more… compact.
In other words, you shrank it.
lines.note: In other words: she says plainly what he is hiding. Shrank is the past of shrink.

lines.text: What I'm trying to say is, it'll fit the cat perfectly.
lines.note: What I'm trying to say is…: he tries again, another way.

lines.text: I'm home! How's my plant doing?
lines.note: I'm home! is what you say when you come in.

lines.text: Well… how do I put this?
lines.note: How do I put this? He is looking for gentle words.

lines.text: Let's just say I thought about it.
lines.note: Let's just say… softens the truth.

lines.text: I don't know how to put this… It's resting.

lines.note: Couch is American English. British English: sofa.
Like is a filler here. Informal: do not write it.
Yeah, but… accepts the point, then objects.

lines.text: There's a spring sticking out! I mean, you can't even sit on it anymore.
lines.note: Sticking out: coming out of the surface. I mean adds force here.

lines.text: Do you see what I'm getting at or not?
lines.note: What I'm getting at = what I mean.

lines.text: All I see is how much a new couch costs.

notes: I mean corrects or sharpens what you just said. Or rather gives a more exact word.
Actually gives the real fact, or the real question. It does not mean 'now'.
In other words says it again plainly. What I'm trying to say is… tries again when the first attempt failed.
How do I put this? and Let's just say… buy time before bad news.
Sort of is a careful yes: partly true.
Like, well and still are spoken words. Do not use like this way in writing.

questions.q: Lucas says the cake is 'different', then changes his word. Which phrase does he use?
questions.why: I mean corrects what you just said: It's… different. I mean, original.

questions.q: Emma says plainly what Lucas did to her sweater. How does she begin?
questions.why: In other words says the same thing in plainer words: you shrank it.

questions.q: Is the plant dead? Lucas gives a careful yes. What does he say?
questions.why: Sort of = partly true. A careful yes.

questions.q: The couch is old, but Lucas adds a point in its favour. What does he say?
questions.why: Yeah, but… accepts the point, then gives the objection.
